newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, lack of coupon pass cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, lack of coupon pass cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended moderately weaker on Wednesday, as the market was disappointed the Federal Reserve did not buy coupons as many had anticipated.
But Treasuries came off their lows late in the session on weaker than expected November auto sales numbers.
The 30-year bond ended at 101-12/32, down 13/32 from Tuesday. Its yield rose to 6.40 percent from 6.37 percent. Shortly before the futures market closed, the bond was down as much as 21/32.

"People have a lot of profits, but they held off taking them because of hopes the market would improve on a coupon pass," explained Michelle Laughlin, chief Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc. When that did not happen, investors booked those profits, she added.

The market spent much of the day trading in narrow ranges, shrugging off the Federal Reserves Beige Book report and the Boskin Commission study on the overstatement of the consumer price index -- both of which were in line with expectations.
Instead, the market was confident the Fed would finally add permanent reserves to the banking system via a coupon pass.
Market participants kept their fingers crossed for a coupon pass until about 1400 EST/1900 GMT, typically the latest time the Fed buys coupons.

"It sounds lame but it seemed to be the driver," said Patrick Dimick, government bond strategist at UBS Securities LLC. He said the disappointment over the lack of a coupon pass was primarily centered in the futures market, in that day traders speculated the Fed would indeed buy.
"When that didn't happen, they had to give up hope," he added.
And, as bond futures fell, the cash market followed.
Traders also said the afternoon decline in stock prices added to the problem. "It was a bit of a wake-up call," said the head bond trader at a primary dealership.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended down nearly 20 points at around 6423, but well off its afternoon low of 6367.
The trader said as year end approaches, it becomes increasingly difficult to attract new buyers, in the process making it hard to continue rallying.
Meanwhile, reports of a Middle East account selling 10-year notes and Asian accounts selling Treasuries due to the dollar's fall against the yen aided the bond market's decline.
Laughlin said it will be difficult for the market to move higher in the future, since upcoming economic news should be stronger rather than weaker.
Wednesday's economic data, though, were seen as mostly neutral.

The Fed's Beige Book said the U.S. economy kept growing moderately in November, with little or no sign of wage and price pressures flaring up. The report said retailers were "modestly optimistic" that the holiday shopping season will be good.

Later, the Boskin Commission reported that its study found the consumer price index overstates inflation by 1.1 percent. The findings were encouraging for the market because if the government follows the commission's recommendations, it would dramatically cut the budget deficit. But, since the results were expected, the bond market shrugged off the report.

But late in the day, Ford Motor Co reported an 11.3 percent drop in car sales in November and a 5.7 percent gain in light truck sales. Combined with poor sales from Chrysler and General Motors earlier in the week, bonds were able to come off lows on hopes retail sales in November will be weak.

Thursday is expected to be a quiet day, players said, as the market awaits the November employment report Friday. If anything, the market could come under more pressure, some believe, because the market is gearing up for a stronger than expected report. A Reuters poll found economists on average predicting a 179,000 rise in non-farm payrolls last month.
Weekly jobless claims and third qaurter unit labor costs and productivity will be released Thursday morning.
Some analysts are still expecting a coupon pass from the Fed on Thursday.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
